lessons.title: Why Your Words Are Everything
lessons.subtitle: Most people use AI like a search engine — that's why they get mediocre results

cards.headline: Two people ask AI the same thing. One gets gold. The other gets garbage. The only difference? How they asked.
cards.body: Most people type into AI the same way they'd Google something — a few vague words and hope for the best. That's the #1 mistake beginners make. Today you'll discover why your words are the most powerful tool in your AI toolkit.
cards.statLabel: better results from specific vs vague prompts (Stanford AI Lab)

cards.headline: AI is a mirror, not a mind reader
cards.body: When you ask AI something vague, it has to guess what you want — and it fills in the gaps with the most generic version possible. When you're specific, it delivers exactly what you need. The quality of your input directly determines the quality of your output.
bullets: ❌ Vague: "Help me write an email" → Generic, forgettable draft
✅ Specific: "Write a warm 3-sentence follow-up email to a client who hasn't replied in 5 days" → Ready to send
The only difference is clarity — and that's a skill you can learn right now

cards.headline: Prompting vs searching — a crucial difference
cards.body: Search engines find pages that already exist. AI generates a brand-new response shaped entirely by your exact words. That's why prompt engineering is its own skill — and why it's worth mastering.
bullets: Google: "email follow-up template" → Shows you articles someone else wrote
AI: "Write a follow-up email for my exact situation" → Creates something just for you
With AI you're not searching for answers — you're directing a creation

cards.headline: The 10-second rule
cards.body: Before sending any prompt, ask yourself: "Could someone with no context understand exactly what I want?" If the answer's no, add one sentence. That single habit will immediately improve 80% of your results.
bullets: ❌ "Write me something good" — what? for who? how long? what tone?
✅ "Write a 3-sentence LinkedIn post about why sleep is underrated for entrepreneurs. Tone: casual and punchy."
More specific = more useful. Every single time.

cards.headline: Your first experiment
cards.body: Open any AI tool — ChatGPT (chat.openai.com) or Claude (claude.ai), both free. Run these two prompts and compare the outputs:
bullets: Prompt A: "Help me write a bio"
Prompt B: "Write a 3-sentence professional bio for a [your job title] who helps [your audience]. Tone: confident but approachable."
Notice how much better Prompt B is — and how little extra effort it took

quiz.question: What's the main reason vague prompts produce poor AI results?
options: AI picks responses randomly from its training data
AI has to guess what you mean and fills the gaps with generic content
Vague prompts trigger safety filters that limit responses
Short prompts use fewer tokens and produce shorter outputs
quiz.explanation: When you're vague, AI doesn't know your goal, audience, tone, or format — so it guesses. It fills in the blanks with the most "average" version of what you might want, which is usually generic and unhelpful. Specificity removes the guesswork and unlocks precision.

quiz.question: How is prompting AI different from searching Google?
options: They work identically — AI is just a smarter search engine
Google generates custom content; AI finds existing pages
AI generates a brand-new personalised response based on your exact words
AI searches the internet and summarises what it finds
quiz.explanation: Search engines retrieve documents that already exist. AI creates a brand-new response from scratch, shaped entirely by your specific prompt. That's why the same tool gives wildly different results to different people — it's responding to your exact words, not retrieving a cached answer.

quiz.question: The "10-second rule" is: before sending a prompt, ask yourself whether someone with no context could understand exactly what you want.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Exactly right. The 10-second rule is a simple mental check: if a stranger read your prompt with zero background knowledge, would they know exactly what output you're looking for? If not, add one sentence of context. This one habit dramatically improves the quality of most AI outputs.

quiz.question: Which of these is the STRONGEST prompt?
options: "Write something for my website"
"Give me some content ideas"
"Write a 100-word homepage headline for a personal finance app helping millennials save their first £1,000. Friendly, motivating tone."
"Make it sound professional"
quiz.explanation: The strongest prompt specifies the task, format (100-word headline), audience (millennials), goal (save first £1,000), and tone (friendly and motivating). All four key ingredients are present. The other options leave too many critical decisions to guesswork — and AI fills those gaps with generic defaults.

lessons.title: Inside the Machine: How AI Reads You
lessons.subtitle: AI isn't understanding your words — it's predicting them. Here's what that means for you

cards.headline: AI isn't understanding you. It's completing you. Once you know the difference, everything changes.
cards.body: Most people think AI reads their prompt like a human — taking in meaning, intent, and context. The reality is more fascinating, and far more useful to understand. Today you'll get the mental model that separates good prompters from great ones.
cards.statLabel: words in GPT-4's training data

cards.headline: Tokens — the building blocks of AI
cards.body: AI doesn't process words the way humans do. It works with "tokens" — small text chunks (roughly ¾ of a word on average). When you type a prompt, AI receives a stream of tokens and its job is to predict the next most likely sequence.
bullets: "Prompt engineering" = roughly 4 tokens
Your whole prompt fits in a "context window" — everything AI can see at once
The more useful context in that window, the more precisely AI can predict what you need

cards.headline: The prediction engine
cards.body: At every step, AI is asking: "Given everything I've seen so far, what's the most likely next token?" It learned from billions of human-written examples — which is why it sounds so human. It's completing patterns from human text at superhuman scale.
bullets: Think autocomplete on your phone — AI is that concept, but vastly more powerful
It's not "thinking" — it's pattern-matching at incredible speed and scale
Clearly written prompts → clearly written outputs (because clear patterns have clear completions)

cards.headline: What this means for your prompts
cards.body: Once you understand AI is a prediction engine, the strategy is clear: structure your prompt so the most likely completion is exactly what you want. The clearer you are, the fewer valid completions exist — and the more useful the one AI picks.
bullets: Vague prompt → thousands of equally likely completions → AI picks an average one
Specific prompt → one clearly right completion → AI nails it
You're not chatting with AI — you're steering its prediction

cards.headline: Peek inside the machine
cards.body: Try this experiment in any AI tool — it reveals how prediction works better than any explanation could:
bullets: Type: "The best way to start a prompt is to..." and let AI finish. It predicts advice based on patterns it learned.
Then try: "As a frustrated user who hates AI, the best way to start a prompt is to..." — notice how the role shifts the prediction
Same starting phrase, very different completions — because context changes what's "most likely"

quiz.question: What does an AI model fundamentally do when you send it a prompt?
options: It searches the internet for the best answer
It retrieves answers from a database of Q&A pairs
It calculates the mathematically correct response
It predicts the most likely next tokens based on patterns from its training data
quiz.explanation: Modern AI models like GPT-4 and Claude are prediction engines. They take your prompt as a sequence of tokens and generate the statistically most likely continuation, based on billions of examples of human text. They don't "look up" answers — they generate new ones that fit the pattern you've set up.

quiz.question: What is the "context window" in AI?
options: The time limit before AI forgets your conversation
The maximum number of characters allowed in a response
A safety filter that screens prompts before processing
Everything AI can "see" in a single interaction — your prompt and the conversation so far
quiz.explanation: The context window is essentially AI's working memory for a conversation. It includes your prompt, any previous messages, and any system instructions. The more useful, relevant context you fit in that window, the better AI can predict what you actually need — which is why context is one of the 4 core prompt ingredients.

quiz.question: True or False: AI genuinely understands the meaning of your words the way a human does.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. AI doesn't "understand" meaning — it predicts patterns. What looks like understanding is extremely sophisticated pattern-matching across billions of text examples. This matters for prompt engineering: you're not explaining something to a person — you're setting up a prediction sequence that leads to your desired output.

quiz.question: Why does adding a specific role ("Act as a marketing expert...") to a prompt change the output?
options: It unlocks a hidden mode in the AI
It shifts what patterns are "most likely" to follow — changing the prediction
It makes AI search specifically within marketing content
It reduces the number of tokens used, making responses faster
quiz.explanation: Because AI is a prediction engine, framing changes what completion is most likely. "As a marketing expert, the key to a great campaign is..." activates patterns from marketing-expert writing in the training data. The role is a context signal that steers the statistical prediction — not a mode switch or a database filter.

lessons.title: The 4 Ingredients of a Perfect Prompt
lessons.subtitle: Task · Context · Format · Tone — every great prompt has all four

cards.headline: Every prompt that gets amazing results has 4 things in common. Every prompt that flops is missing at least one.
cards.body: Great prompts aren't magic — they're a recipe. Once you know the 4 ingredients, you can construct a powerful prompt for almost any task in under a minute. Today you'll learn the framework professionals use every day — and write your first power prompt.
cards.statLabel: ingredients in every great prompt

cards.headline: Ingredient 1: Task — tell AI exactly what to do
cards.body: The Task is the action you want AI to perform. It should start with a clear verb and be as specific as possible. Vague tasks produce vague results. Precise tasks produce precise results.
bullets: ❌ Weak: "Something about my business"
✅ Strong: "Write a 200-word About Us paragraph for my business"
Power verbs: Write · Summarise · Compare · Generate · Rewrite · Explain · Create · List · Analyse · Translate

cards.headline: Ingredient 2: Context — give AI the background it needs
cards.body: AI has no idea who you are, what industry you're in, or who your audience is unless you tell it. Context fills in those blanks. Think of it as briefing a talented freelancer who just walked in the door.
bullets: Who you are: "I'm a fitness coach targeting busy parents"
What it's for: "for a landing page to drive sign-ups for my 8-week programme"
Why it matters: "my audience is time-poor and sceptical of quick fixes"
More relevant context = more tailored output

cards.headline: Ingredients 3 & 4: Format + Tone — control HOW it responds
cards.body: Format tells AI the shape of the output. Tone tells it the voice. Together they determine whether you get a bullet list or an essay, a formal report or a casual caption.
bullets: Format: bullet list · numbered steps · table · paragraph · email · social post · script · summary
Tone: professional · casual · friendly · motivating · authoritative · witty · empathetic · concise
Example: "Format: 5 bullet points. Tone: confident and actionable." — crystal clear.

cards.headline: Build your first 4-ingredient prompt
cards.body: Use this structure and fill in your own details. Then send it to any AI tool and see the difference:
bullets: 1️⃣ Task: "Write a [format, e.g. 3-sentence caption / 200-word email] about [topic]..."
2️⃣ Context: "I'm a [who you are] targeting [your audience] for [what it's for]..."
3️⃣ Format: "Format: [bullet list / short paragraphs / numbered list]"
4️⃣ Tone: "Tone: [how it should sound, e.g. warm, punchy, formal]"
Example: "Write a 3-sentence Instagram caption about meal prep. I'm a nutritionist targeting working mums. Format: 3 short sentences. Tone: practical and encouraging."

quiz.question: Which of the 4 prompt ingredients tells AI WHO you're writing for?
options: Task
Context
Format
Tone
quiz.explanation: Context fills in the background AI needs to tailor its output — including your identity, your audience, and the purpose of the task. Without context, AI writes for a generic imaginary reader. With context, every word is aimed at your real goal.

quiz.question: You want AI to give you a numbered list of 5 steps. Which ingredient controls this?
options: Task
Context
Format
Tone
quiz.explanation: Format tells AI the structure and shape of its output. "Format: numbered list of 5 steps" is a format instruction. Task tells AI what to write about; Format tells it how to present it. Getting both right is the difference between useful output and output you have to reformat yourself.

quiz.question: "Write a warm, encouraging post that makes people feel motivated" — what ingredient is "warm and encouraging" an example of?
options: Task
Context
Format
Tone
quiz.explanation: Tone describes the voice, emotion, and style of the writing. "Warm and encouraging" is a tone instruction. Without a tone, AI defaults to its neutral, somewhat corporate house style. Defining tone clearly ensures the output sounds like you — not like a generic AI.

quiz.question: True or False: For any important task, including all 4 ingredients (Task, Context, Format, Tone) will almost always produce better results than omitting one.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. In practice you can sometimes skip an ingredient if it's genuinely irrelevant — but for any task that matters, all four dramatically improve quality. Think of it as a recipe: you can leave out one ingredient, but the dish is almost always better when you include all four. Once this becomes habit, you'll write great prompts almost automatically.

lessons.title: Build Your First Power Prompt
lessons.subtitle: Put all 4 ingredients together — and write a prompt you'll actually use today

cards.headline: You've learned the theory. Now it's time to build something real — a prompt you can copy, use, and get a great result from right now.
cards.body: Knowing the 4 ingredients is one thing. Assembling them into a prompt that actually delivers is another. Today you'll build your first complete Power Prompt — step by step — and you'll see exactly how the pieces click together.
cards.statLabel: to write a Power Prompt once you know the formula

cards.headline: The Power Prompt Template
cards.body: Here's the exact structure pros use. Fill in the blanks and you have a Power Prompt every time:
bullets: 1️⃣ Task: "[Action verb] a [format] about [topic]..."
2️⃣ Context: "I am a [who you are] and this is for [audience/purpose]..."
3️⃣ Format: "Format: [bullet list / numbered steps / single paragraph / table]"
4️⃣ Tone: "Tone: [word that captures the voice you want]"

cards.headline: See it in action — before and after
cards.body: Here's the same request as a weak prompt vs a Power Prompt. The difference in output quality is enormous:
bullets: ❌ Weak: "Write me a job description for a sales role"

✅ Power Prompt: "Write a 200-word job description for a SaaS Account Executive role at a fast-growing startup. I am the Head of People. Target audience: ambitious mid-career sales professionals. Format: short paragraphs with a bullet list of key responsibilities. Tone: energetic and aspirational."
Same task. Night-and-day output.

cards.headline: The shortcut: start with the end in mind
cards.body: Before writing a single word of your prompt, answer these three questions in your head:
bullets: 🎯 What does the perfect output look like? (That defines Task + Format)
👤 Who is this for and what do they need? (That defines Context)
🗣️ How should it sound? (That defines Tone)
Once you can picture the perfect output, writing the prompt is just describing it to AI

cards.headline: Write your own Power Prompt right now
cards.body: Think of something you actually need to write or create this week. Use the template:
bullets: Fill in: "Write a [format] about [topic]..."
Add: "I am a [role] and this is for [audience/purpose]..."
Specify: "Format: [structure]. Tone: [voice]."
Send it to ChatGPT or Claude — then notice how much better the output is than your usual approach
Keep this prompt. You've just built the foundation of your personal prompt library.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the 4 Power Prompt ingredients?
options: Format → Tone → Task → Context
Context → Task → Tone → Format
Task → Context → Format → Tone
Tone → Context → Format → Task
quiz.explanation: The natural order is Task (what to do) → Context (background it needs) → Format (how to shape the output) → Tone (the voice). Starting with Task anchors the prompt with the action. Context provides the "why" and "who for". Format and Tone then refine how the output looks and sounds. That said, the order matters less than including all four — AI reads the whole prompt before responding.

quiz.question: Before writing a Power Prompt, the most useful first step is to picture what the perfect output looks like.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Exactly right. If you can describe the ideal output in your head — its format, audience, tone, and purpose — writing the prompt is just translating that picture into text. People who struggle with prompts are usually unclear on what they actually want. Starting with the destination makes the directions obvious.

quiz.question: Which of these is the strongest Power Prompt?
options: "Write a bio for me"
"Write a professional bio, keep it short and punchy"
"Write a 3-sentence professional bio for a UX designer specialising in mobile apps. Audience: potential clients on LinkedIn. Tone: confident and approachable."
"Write something for my LinkedIn page about my work in design"
quiz.explanation: Option C includes all 4 Power Prompt ingredients: Task (write a 3-sentence bio), Context (UX designer, mobile apps, potential clients on LinkedIn), Format (3 sentences), and Tone (confident and approachable). The others are missing at least 2 ingredients, so AI has to guess the audience, format, tone, and specific focus — producing generic output.

quiz.question: Why should you keep the Power Prompts you write?
options: So you can submit them as homework
So AI can learn your preferences over time
They form the start of a reusable personal prompt library you can tweak and reuse
They're required for the course certificate
quiz.explanation: A personal prompt library is one of the most valuable things a skilled AI user builds. Instead of rewriting prompts from scratch every time, you refine and reuse proven ones. By Lesson 19 of this course you'll build out that library systematically — but every Power Prompt you save now is a head start.

lessons.title: Tone & Style: The Voice of Your Prompts
lessons.subtitle: Same words, completely different result — tone is more powerful than most people realise

cards.headline: Two prompts. Identical topic. Opposite tones. The outputs are so different, you'd swear they were from two different writers.
cards.body: Most beginners focus entirely on what they're asking for — and completely ignore how it should be said. Tone is often the single change that transforms a mediocre output into one you're genuinely proud of. Today you'll master it.
cards.statLabel: of readers judge content quality primarily by its tone and voice (Nielsen Norman Group)

cards.headline: What "tone" actually means in prompting
cards.body: Tone tells AI the emotional register and personality of the output. It answers the question: "How should this sound?" Without a tone instruction, AI defaults to its neutral house style — which sounds like a slightly corporate, slightly bland version of whatever you asked for.
bullets: Without tone: "Here are five strategies for improving your sleep habits." (Generic)
Tone: casual and encouraging: "Sleep better? Here's the honest truth about what actually works..." (Engaging)
Tone: data-driven and authoritative: "Research across 12 sleep studies identifies five evidence-backed interventions..." (Expert)
Same information. Completely different reader experience.

cards.headline: A tone vocabulary you can use right now
cards.body: Pick one or two tone words per prompt. Combining three or more can create contradictions that confuse the output.
bullets: 🟦 Professional & Formal: authoritative · expert · precise · data-driven · objective
🟩 Warm & Human: friendly · encouraging · empathetic · conversational · supportive
🟨 Energetic & Bold: punchy · direct · confident · motivating · inspiring
🟥 Creative & Distinctive: witty · playful · irreverent · storytelling · poetic

cards.headline: Tone vs Style — a useful distinction
cards.body: Tone describes the emotional register (how it feels). Style describes the structural choices (how it reads). You can combine both in one prompt for maximum control.
bullets: Tone example: "Tone: warm and encouraging"
Style example: "Style: short punchy sentences, no jargon, contractions welcome"
Combined: "Tone: casual and motivating. Style: 2-sentence paragraphs, active voice, avoid corporate buzzwords."
The more specific your tone + style, the closer the first draft gets to what you actually want

cards.headline: The same topic, three tones
cards.body: Open any AI tool. Pick any topic you care about and run all three prompts:
bullets: Prompt 1: "Write 3 sentences about [your topic]. Tone: formal and authoritative."
Prompt 2: "Write 3 sentences about [your topic]. Tone: casual and encouraging."
Prompt 3: "Write 3 sentences about [your topic]. Tone: bold and punchy."
Read all three outputs side by side — the difference will instantly show you why tone matters
Save the tone that fits your brand or your goal. You'll use it in every prompt you write.

quiz.question: What happens when you don't specify a tone in your prompt?
options: AI chooses the most creative tone available
AI mirrors whatever tone you used when writing the prompt
AI defaults to its neutral, slightly corporate house style
AI asks you a follow-up question to clarify the tone
quiz.explanation: Without a tone instruction, AI falls back to its default voice — which tends to be neutral, somewhat formal, and faintly corporate. It's not bad, but it's generic. For any output that needs to sound like a specific person, brand, or emotional register, you must specify tone explicitly. Default mode is the lowest-risk, lowest-impact choice.

quiz.question: True or False: You can combine as many tone words as you want — the more you add, the more control you have.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Combining too many tone words often creates contradictions that confuse the output. "Authoritative, casual, witty, formal, empathetic, and playful" gives AI competing signals — the result is usually incoherent. One or two well-chosen tone words give AI a clear target. Three at most, and only if they reinforce each other.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Tone and Style in prompting?
options: Tone = the topic; Style = the format
Tone = emotional register (how it feels); Style = structural choices (how it reads)
Tone = length of the output; Style = vocabulary level
They mean the same thing — tone and style are interchangeable
quiz.explanation: Tone describes the emotional register and personality of the output — how it makes the reader feel. Style describes structural choices like sentence length, vocabulary, use of contractions, or avoidance of jargon. They're different controls you can use independently or together. "Tone: warm. Style: short sentences, no bullet points" would give you warm, human-feeling prose that reads in a punchy way.

quiz.question: Which tone instruction would work BEST for a formal business report?
options: "Tone: playful and irreverent"
"Tone: data-driven, authoritative, and objective"
"Tone: conversational and casual — write like you're texting a friend"
"Tone: warm and encouraging, like a supportive life coach"
quiz.explanation: A formal business report needs authority, precision, and objectivity — hallmarks of the data-driven, authoritative, objective tone cluster. Playful or irreverent tone would undermine credibility. Conversational or casual tone would make it feel unprofessional. Warm and encouraging works well for coaching content but not formal analysis. Match the tone to the context and audience.

lessons.title: The 7 Mistakes That Ruin Good Prompts
lessons.subtitle: Even experienced users make these — spot them, fix them, never make them again

cards.headline: You can know the 4 ingredients perfectly and still get terrible results. These 7 mistakes are the reason why.
cards.body: Most prompt failures aren't about missing a technique — they're about a handful of predictable errors that are easy to fix once you know them. After today's lesson, you'll catch these mistakes in your own prompts before you send them.
cards.statLabel: mistakes account for 90% of disappointing AI outputs

cards.headline: Mistakes 1 & 2: Too vague + Too much at once
cards.body: The two most common failure modes — and they're opposites of each other.
bullets: ❌ Mistake 1 — Too vague: "Write something for my blog" → No topic, format, audience, or purpose. AI guesses everything wrong.
✅ Fix: Specify at minimum: topic, format, audience, purpose. One sentence of context is enough.
❌ Mistake 2 — Too much at once: "Write a blog post, social media captions, an email newsletter, and a video script about my product launch" → AI can't do four things well simultaneously.
✅ Fix: One task per prompt. Four prompts, four great outputs.

cards.headline: Mistakes 3 & 4: Assuming AI knows you + Contradicting yourself
cards.body: AI has zero memory between sessions — and it can't read your mind even within a session.
bullets: ❌ Mistake 3: "You know what I'm working on — just continue from last time" → AI has no memory across new conversations.
✅ Fix: Re-establish context at the start of every new session. Copy in your key background in 2-3 sentences.
❌ Mistake 4: "Write a formal professional email but keep it super casual and chatty" → Formal and casual are contradictions.
✅ Fix: Pick one. Or be specific: "Professional in structure, warm in tone — no corporate jargon."

cards.headline: Mistakes 5, 6 & 7: Accepting the first draft + Passive voice + Wrong length
cards.body: These three are responsible for most "AI outputs are all the same" frustration.
bullets: ❌ Mistake 5: Taking the first output as final → AI's first attempt is a first draft, not a finished product.
✅ Fix: Use follow-up prompts: "Shorten this by 30%" / "Make this more direct" / "Rewrite the opening to lead with the benefit."
❌ Mistake 6: Not specifying length → AI picks a default length that's often too long or too short.
✅ Fix: "Write exactly 3 sentences" / "150 words max" / "3 bullet points, each under 12 words."
❌ Mistake 7: Passive, uncertain language → "Maybe you could try to write..." gives wishy-washy outputs.
✅ Fix: Be direct. "Write. List. Compare. Summarise." Command tense gets sharper results.

cards.headline: Spot the mistakes
cards.body: Here are 3 real prompts. Before you read on, try to identify which mistake each one is making:
bullets: Prompt A: "Write me a comprehensive detailed in-depth guide to fitness, nutrition, sleep, mental health, morning routines, evening routines, and productivity all in one document." → Which mistake?
Prompt B: "You know the project I told you about last week — just pick up where we left off." → Which mistake?
Prompt C: "Please feel free to maybe try and write something about our company if you wouldn't mind." → Which mistake?
Answers: A = Mistake 2 (too much at once). B = Mistake 3 (AI has no memory). C = Mistake 7 (passive, uncertain language).
Notice how obvious each mistake looks from the outside. That awareness is what stops you making them from the inside.

quiz.question: You ask AI to "write a professional email but keep it super casual and informal." Which mistake is this?
options: Mistake 1 — Too vague
Mistake 2 — Too much at once
Mistake 4 — Contradicting yourself
Mistake 6 — Not specifying length
quiz.explanation: "Professional" and "super casual and informal" are contradictory instructions. AI tries to satisfy both — and usually satisfies neither, producing something awkward and inconsistent. The fix is to pick one register, or be specific about what you actually mean: "Professionally structured, but warm and human in tone — no corporate jargon."

quiz.question: You open a new AI chat and type: "Continue the project from last time — you remember what we discussed." What will happen?
options: AI will recall the conversation from the previous session
AI will access your account history to find the context
AI has no memory across new sessions and will ask for clarification or make things up
AI will generate a new version of the previous output automatically
quiz.explanation: Most AI tools (including ChatGPT and Claude in default mode) have no memory between separate conversations. Each new chat is a blank slate. When you reference something AI has no record of, it either confesses it doesn't know or — more dangerously — fabricates plausible-sounding context. Always re-establish key background at the start of every new session.

quiz.question: True or False: AI's first response to a prompt is usually the best you'll get — refining it makes things worse.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. The first output is a starting point, not a final product. Follow-up prompts are where the real quality lives. "Make this 30% shorter", "Rewrite the opening to hook the reader immediately", "Make this more direct and confident" — each iteration improves the output. Professionals rarely use a first draft as-is. Iteration is the skill that separates good AI users from great ones.

quiz.question: Which of these prompt openers will get the sharpest, most direct result from AI?
options: "Please could you perhaps try and maybe write something about..."
"If you wouldn't mind, it would be great if you could possibly..."
"Write a [format] about [topic]."
"I was kind of hoping you might be able to help me with..."
quiz.explanation: Direct command language — "Write. List. Summarise. Compare." — produces sharper, more decisive outputs than passive or uncertain language. When you hedge with "maybe", "perhaps", "if you wouldn't mind", AI picks up on the tentativeness and often produces similarly vague, hedged output. This is one of the quickest, easiest upgrades you can make to every prompt you write.

cards.headline: The Module 1 Mental Model
cards.body: Everything you've learned so far flows from one simple truth: AI is a prediction engine shaped entirely by your input. The quality of your prompt is the quality of your output. Here's the complete foundation in one view:
bullets: 1️⃣ Words matter — specificity beats vagueness every single time
2️⃣ AI predicts, not understands — structure your prompt to make the right prediction obvious
3️⃣ The 4 ingredients: Task · Context · Format · Tone — all four, every important prompt
4️⃣ Tone is a lever — one word change transforms the entire output
5️⃣ Avoid the 7 mistakes — vague, overloaded, contradictory, passive, no length, no memory, accept first draft
6️⃣ Iterate — the first draft is a starting point, not the destination

cards.headline: What changes in Module 2
cards.body: Module 1 was about writing better individual prompts. Module 2 is about techniques — named, repeatable approaches that professionals use to unlock capabilities most people don't know exist.
bullets: Role Prompting: assign AI a persona and watch the output transform
Chain of Thought: make AI show its reasoning and catch its own errors
Few-Shot Prompting: give AI examples and it mirrors your exact style
The Iteration Loop: a 3-step process that turns first drafts into finals
Negative Prompting: tell AI what NOT to do for cleaner results
Context Stacking: build layered prompts that give AI everything it needs in one go

cards.headline: Your Foundation Prompt Formula
cards.body: Commit this to memory. It's the starting point for every advanced technique you'll learn in Module 2:
bullets: 📌 [Action verb] a [format] about [topic]
📌 I am a [who you are] and this is for [audience/purpose]
📌 Format: [structure]. Tone: [voice].
📌 Then: iterate with follow-up prompts until it's right
Every Module 2 technique slots INTO this structure — it doesn't replace it

cards.headline: The Module 1 Challenge
cards.body: Write a single prompt that uses ALL 4 ingredients and avoids ALL 7 mistakes. Here's a scenario to work with:
bullets: You're a freelance graphic designer launching a new service helping small businesses with their brand identity
You need an Instagram caption announcing your new service launch
Requirements: 3 sentences, exciting but professional tone, call to action included
Write the prompt. Check it against the 4 ingredients. Check it against the 7 mistakes. Then send it to AI.
If your output is genuinely post-worthy, you've passed Module 1.

quiz.question: What is the single most important thing to understand about how AI processes your prompt?
options: AI searches the internet for the best available answer
AI selects from a database of pre-written responses
AI predicts the most likely next tokens based on patterns from its training data
AI uses logic and reasoning to calculate the correct answer
quiz.explanation: This is the foundational insight of Module 1. AI is a prediction engine — it predicts the most statistically likely continuation of your prompt, based on billions of examples in its training data. Understanding this explains everything: why specificity works, why tone matters, why structure helps, and why the first draft is never perfect. You're not communicating with a mind — you're steering a prediction.

quiz.question: Which of the 4 prompt ingredients is most often missing from beginner prompts?
options: Task — beginners forget to say what they want AI to do
Context — beginners forget to tell AI who they are, the audience, and the purpose
Format — beginners always specify exactly how they want output structured
Tone — beginners naturally include tone in every prompt
quiz.explanation: Context is the most commonly missing ingredient. Beginners naturally write the task — "write me an email" — but forget to tell AI who it's for, who's writing it, and why it matters. Without context, AI writes for a generic imaginary person. Adding even two sentences of context — "I'm a [role] writing to [audience] for [purpose]" — dramatically improves relevance and usefulness.

quiz.question: True or False: Once you master the 4-ingredient formula, you no longer need to use follow-up prompts — the first draft will be right.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Even perfect prompts produce first drafts, not finished products. The 4-ingredient formula dramatically improves your starting point — but iteration is where final quality lives. "Shorten by 30%", "Make the opening punchier", "Add a specific example in paragraph 2" — these follow-up prompts are how pros turn good into great. Iteration is a skill, not a workaround.

quiz.question: You're about to send this prompt: "Write something about our company values for the website." Which two ingredients are missing?
options: Task and Context
Context and Tone
Format and Tone
Task and Format
quiz.explanation: The Task is present (write about company values) and Context is partially there (for the website). But Format is missing — should this be a paragraph? A bullet list? A hero tagline? And Tone is missing — should this be formal, warm, inspiring? Without Format and Tone, AI will guess — and it usually guesses wrong for your specific brand. Adding "Format: 3 short paragraphs. Tone: inspiring and human." transforms this into a Power Prompt.

lessons.title: Role Prompting: Give AI a Job Title
lessons.subtitle: One sentence transforms AI from a generalist into a specialist. Here's how.

cards.headline: What if you could hire a world-class expert — a CMO, a Harvard professor, a top lawyer — for any task, any time, for free? Role prompting does exactly that.
cards.body: Role prompting is the technique that most surprises beginners when they first try it. By assigning AI a specific expert identity before your task, you activate different patterns from its training data — patterns from expert writing in that field. The results are dramatically more specialised and authoritative.
cards.statLabel: improvement in output quality from role prompting (MIT AI Lab, 2023)

cards.headline: How role prompting works
cards.body: When you tell AI "Act as a [specific expert]", you're steering its prediction toward the patterns of how that expert would write and think. The role functions as a powerful context signal that activates domain-specific knowledge and style.
bullets: Without role: "Explain the key risks of launching a startup" → Generic advice from no particular perspective
With role: "Act as a venture capitalist with 20 years of experience. Explain the key risks of launching a startup from your perspective." → Specific, nuanced, investment-savvy insight
Same question. Completely different level of expertise in the output.

cards.headline: The anatomy of a role prompt
cards.body: The most effective role prompts have three components. The more specific the role, the more focused the output:
bullets: 1️⃣ The title: "Act as a [specific role]" — not just "expert" but the exact type of expert
2️⃣ The experience/context: "with [X years of experience / specialism in Y]" — anchors the role
3️⃣ The perspective: "from your perspective as..." or "using your expertise in..." — activates the right lens
Example: "Act as a UX designer with 10 years of experience designing mobile apps for Gen Z users. Review this onboarding flow and identify friction points from your perspective."

cards.headline: Roles that unlock the best results
cards.body: Some roles are dramatically more useful than others. Here are high-value roles worth memorising:
bullets: 💼 Business: "Act as a McKinsey strategy consultant" · "Act as a CFO of a fast-scaling startup"
✍️ Writing: "Act as an editor at The Economist" · "Act as a direct response copywriter"
🎓 Teaching: "Act as a patient teacher explaining this to a 12-year-old" · "Act as a Socratic tutor"
⚖️ Critical: "Act as a devil's advocate" · "Act as a senior lawyer reviewing this contract"
🔬 Research: "Act as a data scientist" · "Act as a market research analyst"

cards.headline: Three roles, one question
cards.body: Pick any question about a topic you're working on right now. Then ask it three times, each with a different role:
bullets: Prompt 1: "Act as a [domain expert]. [Your question.]"
Prompt 2: "Act as a devil's advocate. [Same question — push back on any assumptions.]"
Prompt 3: "Act as a patient teacher explaining this to someone with zero background. [Same question.]"
Notice how three roles produce three genuinely different, useful perspectives on the same topic
This technique is how pros use AI as a thinking partner, not just a writing tool

quiz.question: Why does assigning AI a role change the quality of its output?
options: It unlocks premium content from the AI's database
It activates domain-specific writing patterns from AI's training data, steering predictions toward expert-level responses
It makes AI try harder because it feels a sense of responsibility
It limits AI to only answering questions in that specific domain
quiz.explanation: Role prompting works because AI is a prediction engine. "Act as a VC with 20 years of experience" is a context signal that makes expert VC-style writing patterns more likely to appear in the prediction. AI has been trained on billions of documents — including expert content in almost every field. A role activates those specific patterns rather than the generic average.

quiz.question: Which is the STRONGER role prompt?
options: "Act as an expert."
"Act as a professional."
"Act as a direct response copywriter with 15 years of experience writing email campaigns for e-commerce brands."
"Act as someone who knows a lot about marketing."
quiz.explanation: Specificity is everything in role prompting. "Expert" and "professional" are so vague they barely steer the prediction at all. "Direct response copywriter with 15 years of experience writing email campaigns for e-commerce brands" gives AI a precise identity that activates very specific writing patterns — the persuasive, conversion-focused style of direct response copywriting. More specific role = more focused output.

quiz.question: True or False: You should only use role prompting for technical or specialised topics — it's too complicated for everyday writing tasks.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Role prompting is one of the most versatile techniques and works brilliantly for everyday tasks. "Act as a patient editor" for any writing, "Act as a persuasive copywriter" for social posts, "Act as a teacher explaining this simply" for learning anything — these are daily-use roles. You don't need a technical topic to benefit. Any time you want a specific perspective or style, a role prompt delivers it.

quiz.question: You want AI to find flaws in a business idea you're excited about. Which role would work best?
options: "Act as an enthusiastic startup cheerleader"
"Act as a devil's advocate and challenge every assumption in this idea"
"Act as a creative brainstormer"
"Act as a motivational coach"
quiz.explanation: When you want critical thinking and flaw-finding, the devil's advocate role is purpose-built for it. It directs AI to actively seek problems, challenge assumptions, and push back — which is exactly what you need to stress-test an idea. An enthusiastic cheerleader, brainstormer, or motivational coach would all bias AI toward positive, supportive output — the last thing you want when evaluating risks.

lessons.title: Chain of Thought: Make AI Show Its Work
lessons.subtitle: The technique that catches AI's errors before they reach you

cards.headline: AI can give you the right answer for the wrong reasons — and you'd never know. Chain of Thought prompting fixes that by making AI show its reasoning, step by step.
cards.body: This is one of the most powerful and least-used techniques in prompt engineering. By adding five simple words to your prompt — "think through this step by step" — you can dramatically improve AI's accuracy, catch errors early, and get answers you can actually verify and trust.
cards.statLabel: accuracy improvement on complex reasoning tasks with Chain of Thought (Google DeepMind)

cards.headline: Why AI makes reasoning errors — and how CoT fixes them
cards.body: AI doesn't 'think' before answering — it predicts the most likely response immediately. For simple tasks that's fine. For complex problems — multi-step analysis, decisions, calculations — that predict-first approach can jump to plausible-sounding but wrong conclusions.
bullets: Without CoT: AI produces a confident-sounding answer that skips critical reasoning steps
With CoT: AI works through each step, catching its own errors in the process
The key insight: making AI 'show its work' forces it to follow the reasoning chain humans use
Errors that would be invisible in a summary become obvious in a step-by-step breakdown

cards.headline: How to activate Chain of Thought
cards.body: There are three levels of CoT prompting — from simple to comprehensive. Start with Level 1 and work up when needed:
bullets: Level 1 — Simple trigger: Add "Think through this step by step before giving your answer."
Level 2 — Structured: "Break your reasoning into numbered steps. Show each step before reaching a conclusion."
Level 3 — Full CoT: "Think through this step by step. After each step, check your reasoning. Only give your final answer after completing all steps."
For most tasks, Level 1 is enough. Use Level 3 for high-stakes decisions or complex analysis.

cards.headline: When Chain of Thought is most valuable
cards.body: CoT isn't needed for simple requests — it adds unnecessary length for basic tasks. It's most powerful in these scenarios:
bullets: 🔢 Maths & calculations: AI makes arithmetic errors without CoT — step-by-step catches them
⚖️ Decisions & trade-offs: "Should I do X or Y?" — CoT surfaces the reasoning behind the recommendation
📊 Analysis & research: Complex data interpretation benefits from visible reasoning chains
🧩 Multi-step problems: Any task with dependencies where an early error cascades into bigger errors
✅ Fact-checking: Ask AI to reason through each claim — hallucinations become easier to spot

cards.headline: See the difference in real time
cards.body: Run these two prompts on any complex question you're curious about right now. Notice the difference in quality and trustworthiness:
bullets: Prompt A: "[Your complex question] — give me your answer."
Prompt B: "[Same question] — think through this step by step before giving your answer. Show each reasoning step."
Compare the two outputs. Which one do you trust more? Which one could you verify?
Try it with: a business decision, a maths problem, a pros/cons analysis, or a strategic question
You'll find Prompt B answers are not just longer — they're genuinely more reliable

quiz.question: Why can AI give a confident but wrong answer without Chain of Thought prompting?
options: AI deliberately simplifies complex answers to be more user-friendly
AI predicts the most likely response immediately — skipping intermediate reasoning steps that humans use
AI lacks the data to answer complex questions correctly
Complex questions trigger safety filters that prevent full answers
quiz.explanation: AI is a prediction engine — it predicts the most likely response immediately, without 'thinking through' the problem the way a human expert would. For simple tasks, this works well. For complex, multi-step problems, this shortcut produces plausible-sounding but sometimes flawed answers. Chain of Thought forces AI to follow the reasoning chain — which catches errors that direct prediction misses.

quiz.question: What is the simplest Chain of Thought trigger you can add to any prompt?
options: "Be extra careful with this one."
"Double-check your answer before replying."
"Think through this step by step before giving your answer."
"Make sure you're accurate."
quiz.explanation: "Think through this step by step" is the cleanest, most research-validated CoT trigger. It directly instructs AI to decompose its reasoning rather than jumping to a prediction. "Be careful" and "make sure you're accurate" are vague instructions that don't change how AI generates its response — they just add noise. Step-by-step is the key phrase that restructures the output.

quiz.question: True or False: You should use Chain of Thought for every prompt — it always improves results.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Chain of Thought adds length and structure to AI's output — which is valuable for complex reasoning but unnecessary for simple tasks. Asking AI to "write a 3-word tagline — think through this step by step" produces a rambling process description when you just needed three words. Use CoT selectively: complex analysis, decisions, maths, fact-checking, or any multi-step problem where an early error would cascade.

quiz.question: You ask AI: "Is it better for my business to raise prices now or wait until Q4?" — which level of CoT would you use?
options: No CoT — this is a simple question that doesn't need it
Level 1 — Add "Think through this step by step" for a solid reasoning chain
Level 3 — "Think through step by step, check each step, only give conclusion after all steps" — high-stakes decisions deserve full CoT
CoT doesn't work for business decisions — only for maths
quiz.explanation: A business pricing decision is high-stakes, multi-factor, and potentially irreversible — exactly where full Level 3 CoT pays off. You want to see AI reason through: market conditions, competitor behaviour, customer psychology, cash flow implications, and timing trade-offs — checking each step. A snap answer from AI on a decision like this carries real risk. Full CoT surfaces the reasoning you need to verify before acting.

lessons.title: Few-Shot Prompting: Teach by Example
lessons.subtitle: Show AI exactly what you want — and it mirrors your style perfectly

cards.headline: Describing what you want is hard. Showing AI two or three examples of what you want? That's instant style-matching — every single time.
cards.body: Few-shot prompting is the technique that finally solves the "it doesn't sound like me" problem. Instead of trying to describe your style in words, you demonstrate it. AI picks up the pattern from your examples and replicates it precisely. It's the closest thing to cloning your voice.
cards.statLabel: higher style consistency when using examples vs description alone (OpenAI research)

cards.headline: Zero-shot vs Few-shot — what's the difference?
cards.body: Most people use AI in zero-shot mode without realising it — they just describe what they want. Few-shot adds examples before the task, which transforms the output:
bullets: 🎯 Zero-shot: "Write a tweet about AI productivity" → AI guesses what style you mean
🎯 Few-shot: "Here are 3 tweets I love: [example 1] [example 2] [example 3]. Now write one about AI productivity in the same style." → AI mirrors exactly
The examples act as a style brief that's worth a thousand description words
One example is good. Two or three is almost always better.

cards.headline: How to structure a few-shot prompt
cards.body: The pattern is simple: examples first, then task. Here's the exact template:
bullets: 1️⃣ Introduction: "Here are [number] examples of [what they are]:"
2️⃣ Examples: Label each clearly — "Example 1:", "Example 2:", "Example 3:"
3️⃣ Task: "Now write [the same thing] about [new topic] in the same style."
Pro tip: Your examples should be as close to the quality you want as possible — AI extrapolates from them, so good examples produce great outputs

cards.headline: Where few-shot prompting excels
cards.body: Some tasks benefit far more from examples than descriptions. These are the top use cases:
bullets: ✍️ Brand voice: Use 2-3 pieces of your existing content — AI writes in your exact style
📱 Social posts: Examples of posts that performed well → AI replicates the formula
📧 Email templates: Share examples of your best emails → AI matches tone and structure
📝 Formatting: Show AI the exact layout you want → it follows it precisely
🎯 Classification: "Label each of these as [category]. Here are examples of each..." → near-perfect accuracy

cards.headline: Clone your writing style in 3 minutes
cards.body: Find 2-3 pieces of your own writing that you're proud of — emails, posts, messages, anything. Then:
bullets: Paste them into AI with: "Here are 3 examples of how I write:"
Label each: "Example 1:", "Example 2:", "Example 3:"
Then add your task: "Now write [new piece] about [new topic] in my exact style."
Read the output — notice how it sounds more like you than any AI output you've gotten before
Save this as your Brand Voice Template. You'll use it constantly.

quiz.question: What is the core principle behind few-shot prompting?
options: Sending AI multiple prompts in one message to save time
Using examples to show AI the exact style or pattern you want, so it can replicate it
Giving AI fewer instructions so it has more creative freedom
Limiting the number of tokens in each prompt for faster responses
quiz.explanation: Few-shot prompting works by demonstration rather than description. Instead of trying to describe your desired style in words (which is hard), you show AI examples that embody that style. AI's pattern-recognition then extrapolates from your examples to new content. Showing beats telling — and the more precise your examples, the more precisely AI mirrors them.

quiz.question: You want AI to write social posts in your exact brand voice. Which approach will produce the best result?
options: Tell AI: "Write in a friendly, conversational, punchy style with short sentences"
Tell AI: "Match my brand voice exactly"
Share 3 of your best-performing posts as examples, then ask AI to write a new one in the same style
Ask AI to guess your brand voice from your company name
quiz.explanation: Examples beat descriptions every time for style matching. Describing your voice — "friendly, conversational, punchy" — gives AI broad signals that produce generic interpretations. Showing AI 3 real examples of your best posts gives it the actual patterns of your specific voice: your sentence rhythm, vocabulary choices, hook structure, and natural cadence. AI extrapolates with precision what it can't reliably infer from adjectives.

quiz.question: True or False: One example is always enough for few-shot prompting — more examples don't improve results.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. One example is better than zero, but two or three examples dramatically improve consistency and accuracy. One example might be ambiguous — AI can't always tell which features of a single example are the important patterns to replicate. Two or three examples show AI what's consistent across them, which is the style signal. For brand voice especially, three examples is the sweet spot.

quiz.question: What makes few-shot prompting especially powerful for brand voice?
options: It makes AI search the internet for similar brand content
It bypasses AI's safety filters for more creative freedom
Real examples capture nuances of style — rhythm, vocabulary, structure — that are nearly impossible to describe in words
It trains AI permanently on your brand so future prompts recognise your voice automatically
quiz.explanation: Your writing voice is made up of dozens of subtle patterns — sentence length, punctuation choices, transition phrases, how you open paragraphs, what vocabulary you favour. These are almost impossible to describe fully in words, but they're immediately visible in your actual writing. Few-shot prompting lets AI read your real examples and extract those patterns directly, producing outputs that match your voice far more closely than any description could.

lessons.title: The Iteration Loop: From First Draft to Final
lessons.subtitle: The 3-step loop that pros use to turn any AI output into something excellent

cards.headline: The biggest lie in AI: "Just ask and it'll be perfect." The truth: great AI output is always the result of 2-4 targeted follow-up prompts. Here's the exact system.
cards.body: Every advanced AI user knows this: the first draft is raw material, not the finished product. The skill that separates mediocre from excellent AI output isn't writing the perfect first prompt — it's knowing exactly how to refine what you get. Today you'll learn the Iteration Loop.
cards.statLabel: better quality after 3 targeted follow-up prompts vs accepting the first draft

cards.headline: The 3-step Iteration Loop
cards.body: The loop is simple, repeatable, and works for any type of content. Once you internalise it, you'll never settle for a mediocre first draft again:
bullets: 1️⃣ ASSESS — Read the output critically. What's good? What's missing? What's off?
2️⃣ DIRECT — Give one specific follow-up instruction targeting the main issue
3️⃣ VERIFY — Check if the issue is resolved. Repeat for the next issue.
Rule: one change per follow-up. Multiple changes in one prompt lead to inconsistent results.
Most tasks are done in 2-3 loops. Complex work might take 4-5.

cards.headline: The follow-up prompt toolkit
cards.body: These are the most powerful follow-up prompts — save these for reuse:
bullets: 📏 Length: "Shorten by 30%" / "Expand the second section to 100 words" / "Keep to 3 sentences max"
🎯 Focus: "Lead with the most important benefit, not the process" / "Cut everything after [X] — it's not needed"
🔊 Tone: "Make this 20% more direct" / "Soften the opening — it feels too aggressive" / "Add more warmth"
💡 Specificity: "Replace the generic examples with specific ones from the tech industry" / "Add a concrete statistic to support this"
✂️ Edit mode: "Remove all instances of corporate jargon" / "Replace every passive sentence with an active one"

cards.headline: The critical feedback formula
cards.body: Vague feedback produces vague revisions. Here's the formula for a follow-up prompt that always works:
bullets: ❌ Weak: "Make this better"
❌ Weak: "I don't like it — redo it"
✅ Strong: "[Specific problem] + [Specific instruction]"
Example: "The opening is too passive — rewrite the first sentence to start with a strong action or surprising fact."
Example: "This is 40 words too long — cut it to 120 words by removing the background context in paragraph 2."
Diagnose the problem first. Then prescribe the fix.

cards.headline: Run the full Iteration Loop
cards.body: Take any output you've previously generated — or generate a new one now. Then run 3 full loops:
bullets: Loop 1: Fix the biggest structural issue (length, format, missing information)
Loop 2: Fix the tone or voice (too formal, not punchy enough, add a hook)
Loop 3: Polish the specifics (replace generic with specific, cut filler words, strengthen the ending)
Compare your Loop 3 output to the original first draft
That difference is the Iteration Loop in action — and it works every single time

quiz.question: What is the core principle of the Iteration Loop?
options: Write the perfect prompt the first time so you never need to follow up
Accept AI's first output — further prompts make things worse
Use one specific follow-up prompt at a time to progressively improve the output toward your goal
Always ask AI to completely rewrite from scratch if you're not happy
quiz.explanation: The Iteration Loop is built on progressive refinement — not perfection on the first attempt. One specific follow-up prompt at a time keeps changes targeted and predictable. Asking for multiple changes at once, or requesting a full rewrite, often loses what was good in the previous version. Assess what's wrong, direct one specific fix, verify it worked, repeat.

quiz.question: Which follow-up prompt will produce the most useful revision?
options: "Make this better"
"I don't like it, try again"
"The opening paragraph buries the main benefit — rewrite it to lead with what the reader gains in the first sentence"
"Can you please try to maybe improve this a bit if you can?"
quiz.explanation: Specific feedback produces specific improvements. "The opening paragraph buries the main benefit — rewrite it to lead with what the reader gains in the first sentence" diagnoses the exact problem and prescribes the exact fix. AI knows exactly what to change and what to keep. Vague prompts like "make this better" or "try again" give AI no signal about what specifically is wrong, so it guesses — often making different trade-offs rather than genuine improvements.

quiz.question: Why should you make only ONE change per follow-up prompt?
options: AI can only process one instruction per message
Multiple changes at once make AI charge more tokens
Multiple changes lead to unpredictable results — you can't tell which instruction caused which output change
It's a style preference — multiple changes work just as well
quiz.explanation: When you ask for multiple changes simultaneously — "shorten it, make it punchier, add more examples, and change the tone" — you can't tell which change caused which result. If the output is now worse, you don't know which instruction to reverse. One change at a time gives you full control: you can confirm each improvement before moving to the next. It also prevents AI from over-editing and losing what was already good.

quiz.question: True or False: If the first draft is broadly good, it's faster to just use it rather than running the Iteration Loop.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False — but it's a nuanced false. If "broadly good" means you genuinely can't improve it, then yes, ship it. But in practice, "broadly good" usually means "acceptable but not excellent" — and one or two targeted follow-up prompts take 30 seconds and dramatically improve the output. The loop isn't about perfectionism; it's about the quick wins that separate good from genuinely impressive. Most content benefits from at least one loop.

lessons.title: Negative Prompting: Tell AI What NOT to Do
lessons.subtitle: The fastest way to eliminate the things that always annoy you about AI output

cards.headline: "Avoid corporate buzzwords." "No filler phrases." "Don't use bullet points." Five words of instruction can eliminate the most common AI annoying habits permanently.
cards.body: Most people only tell AI what TO do. The pros also tell it what NOT to do. Negative prompting is a precision tool for cutting out the predictable patterns that make AI output sound generic — the watered-down disclaimers, the clichéd transitions, the over-enthusiasm. Today you'll build your personal exclusion list.
cards.statLabel: of AI "generic output" is caused by habits you can eliminate with a single negative instruction

cards.headline: Why AI has annoying default habits
cards.body: AI's defaults come from its training data — billions of documents that include a lot of mediocre corporate writing. Without instruction, AI gravitates toward the most common patterns in that writing. Negative prompting breaks those patterns.
bullets: Opening with "Certainly! Here's..." → Add: "Don't start with an affirmation like 'Certainly' or 'Of course'"
Constant hedging: "It's important to note that..." → Add: "Avoid hedge phrases and qualifiers"
Generic transitions: "In conclusion...", "Furthermore..." → Add: "No transitional filler words"
The "As an AI..." disclaimer → Add: "Don't mention that you're an AI"
Over-enthusiasm: "Absolutely!", "Great question!" → Add: "No sycophantic responses"

cards.headline: How to structure negative prompting
cards.body: Add a "Do NOT" section at the end of your prompt. It acts as a final filter on everything AI generates:
bullets: Simple: Add a line at the end of your prompt: "Do NOT: [list of exclusions]"
Example: "Do NOT: use bullet points, start with 'Certainly', include disclaimers, use passive voice, or exceed 200 words."
For recurring prompts: Build a standard exclusion block you paste into every prompt
For brand content: Add your specific brand no-nos — jargon your company avoids, phrases that feel off-brand

cards.headline: Your Master Exclusion List
cards.body: Here's a starter exclusion list based on the most common complaints about AI output. Customise it for your needs:
bullets: 🚫 Structure: "No bullet points" / "No numbered lists" / "No headers" (when you want prose)
🚫 Language: "No corporate jargon" / "No buzzwords like 'synergy', 'leverage', 'robust'" / "No passive voice"
🚫 AI habits: "Don't start with 'Certainly' or 'Of course'" / "No 'As an AI' disclaimers" / "No sycophantic openers"
🚫 Length: "No padding or filler sentences" / "Don't repeat the question back to me" / "No conclusion summaries"
🚫 Tone: "Avoid hedging language" / "No over-qualification" / "Don't soften every statement"

cards.headline: Build your personal exclusion list
cards.body: Think back to the AI outputs that have annoyed you most. What were the recurring issues? Now turn those into a reusable block:
bullets: Write 3-5 things AI does that consistently annoy you or feel off-brand
Turn each into a clear negative instruction: "Do NOT [specific habit]"
Add this block to your next prompt and compare the output to what you'd usually get
Save this as your Personal Exclusion Block — paste it into any important prompt
Tip: Less is more. A focused list of 3-5 exclusions beats a sprawling list of 15.

quiz.question: Why does AI have default habits like starting with "Certainly!" or over-using bullet points?
options: AI is programmed with these habits for user-friendliness
These patterns appear frequently in AI's training data, making them statistically likely predictions
These habits are safety features that can't be turned off
AI developers intentionally designed these responses for a better user experience
quiz.explanation: AI predicts based on patterns in its training data. Phrases like "Certainly!" and heavy bullet-point formatting appear constantly in corporate writing, help docs, and AI-generated content that fed back into training. Without instructions to avoid them, they're among the statistically likely predictions. Negative prompting directly overrides those statistical defaults — telling AI that these patterns are off the table.

quiz.question: Where should you place the "Do NOT" section in a prompt?
options: At the very beginning, before the task
In the middle, after the context
At the end, as a final filter on everything above
It doesn't matter — AI reads the whole prompt before generating anyway
quiz.explanation: Placing the Do NOT section at the end positions it as a final constraint that applies to everything above — it acts as a filter over the whole output. While AI does read the full prompt, recency matters in practice: instructions at the end of a prompt receive slightly more weight as they're closer to where the prediction starts. End placement also makes prompts more readable — positive instructions first, then the exclusion list.

quiz.question: True or False: A longer exclusion list (15+ items) is always better than a short one — more exclusions means cleaner output.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. A focused list of 3-5 high-impact exclusions outperforms a sprawling list of 15. Too many exclusions create competing constraints that can confuse the output or make AI overly cautious about what it can write at all. Focus on the 3-5 habits that most often ruin your outputs. Those targeted exclusions will produce dramatically cleaner results than an exhaustive list of every possible thing you don't want.

quiz.question: You want AI to write clean, flowing prose — but it always defaults to bullet points. What's the most direct fix?
options: Ask AI to "write better"
Use a different AI tool
Add "Do NOT use bullet points or numbered lists" at the end of your prompt
Specify a tone — tone controls formatting
quiz.explanation: Bullet points are one of AI's strongest formatting defaults — it often uses them even when prose would serve better. The most direct fix is a clear negative instruction: "Do NOT use bullet points or numbered lists." Tone instructions don't reliably change formatting. Asking AI to "write better" doesn't communicate what you want. A single negative instruction targeting the specific habit is always the fastest, most reliable solution.

lessons.title: Context Stacking: Build the Perfect Brief
lessons.subtitle: Layer context like a pro — so AI understands your world before it writes a word

cards.headline: The best AI outputs don't come from better prompts — they come from AI that knows you, your audience, your goals, and your constraints before it starts.
cards.body: Context stacking is how professionals turn AI into a specialist who understands their exact situation. Instead of rebuilding context from scratch every session, you create a layered brief — stacked in the right order — that you paste once to set AI up perfectly for any task that follows.
cards.statLabel: of context that transform AI from generalist to specialist

cards.headline: The 5 layers of context
cards.body: Each layer adds a different dimension that sharpens AI's output. Stack them in order — each layer builds on the one before:
bullets: 1️⃣ Identity: Who you are — your role, background, expertise level
2️⃣ Audience: Who you're writing for — demographics, knowledge level, pain points
3️⃣ Goal: What you're trying to achieve — the outcome, not just the task
4️⃣ Constraints: Limits and requirements — word count, format, platform, brand rules
5️⃣ Style: Voice and tone preferences — examples of writing you admire (linking to few-shot)

cards.headline: A stacked context brief in practice
cards.body: Here's how a context stack looks for a real task — notice how each layer adds specificity:
bullets: 1️⃣ Identity: "I'm a B2B SaaS founder with a background in finance, not marketing."
2️⃣ Audience: "My audience is CFOs at mid-sized companies — analytical, sceptical of hype, time-poor."
3️⃣ Goal: "I want to generate demo requests, not just educate — every piece should end with a low-friction CTA."
4️⃣ Constraints: "Max 150 words. LinkedIn format. No industry jargon. No bullet points."
5️⃣ Style: "Write like this example: [paste example post]"
Task follows: "Now write a post about why CFOs overpay for their current FP&A tools."

cards.headline: Your reusable Context Stack template
cards.body: The real power of context stacking is saving it. Build once, reuse forever:
bullets: Create a document called "My AI Context Stack" with your 5 layers filled in
For each major project or client, create a project-specific stack
Start every important AI session by pasting your relevant context stack
Update the stack when your goals or audience change — not every session
Pro tip: Keep each layer to 1-2 sentences. Precision beats length.

cards.headline: Build your Context Stack right now
cards.body: Spend 5 minutes filling in these 5 layers for your most common AI use case:
bullets: 1️⃣ Identity: "I am a [role] with [background/expertise]..."
2️⃣ Audience: "My audience is [who they are, what they care about, what they struggle with]..."
3️⃣ Goal: "My goal is [outcome — what I want people to feel/do/believe]..."
4️⃣ Constraints: "Requirements: [format, word count, platform, brand rules]..."
5️⃣ Style: "Write in this voice: [paste one example or describe key style traits]"
Save this. Paste it at the start of your next AI session and notice the difference.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of context stacking?
options: To make prompts longer so AI has more to work with
To layer five specific types of context in order, so AI understands your full situation before generating output
To replace the 4-ingredient formula with a more advanced system
To reduce the number of follow-up prompts needed by overwhelming AI with information
quiz.explanation: Context stacking is about layering the right types of context — identity, audience, goal, constraints, style — in a structured order. Each layer sharpens AI's understanding of a different dimension of your situation. The result is output that's tailored to you, your audience, and your goals from the very first response. It doesn't replace the 4-ingredient formula — it supercharges the Context ingredient of it.

quiz.question: Which layer of context is most commonly missing from beginner AI sessions?
options: Identity — beginners forget to say who they are
Audience — beginners rarely tell AI who they're writing for or what that audience cares about
Constraints — beginners always specify word counts and formats
Style — beginners naturally include examples of writing they like
quiz.explanation: Audience is the most commonly missing layer. Most people tell AI what they want to write about but forget to describe who they're writing for — their knowledge level, what they care about, what objections they have, and what outcome they need. Without audience context, AI writes for a generic imaginary reader. The moment you describe your real audience precisely, the specificity and relevance of AI's output transforms.

quiz.question: How often should you update your saved Context Stack?
options: Every session — context should always be fresh
Never — once created, the stack is permanent
When your goals, audience, or constraints genuinely change — not for routine tasks
Monthly, as a scheduled review
quiz.explanation: Your Context Stack should be stable enough to reuse without rewriting every session — that's the whole point. Update it when something material changes: you're targeting a new audience, your goal has shifted, you've rebranded, or your constraints are different. For routine work, paste the same stack at the start of each session. The stack is a living document that evolves with your work, not a daily writing exercise.

quiz.question: True or False: Context stacking replaces the 4-ingredient formula (Task · Context · Format · Tone).
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Context stacking is an expansion of the Context ingredient in the 4-ingredient formula — it goes deeper into what 'context' means. You still need Task, Format, and Tone for each individual prompt. Think of it as: your Context Stack sets the standing brief (who you are, who you're writing for, your goals), and each individual prompt adds the Task + Format + Tone for that specific piece. The two systems work together, not instead of each other.

lessons.title: Module 2 Checkpoint: Techniques Mastered
lessons.subtitle: Six professional techniques locked in — now combine them into your power stack

cards.headline: You've just learned the six techniques that separate casual AI users from people who get genuinely impressive results. Now let's lock them in — and combine them.
cards.body: Module 2 covered the named, battle-tested techniques that professionals use every day. Each one is powerful alone. Combined, they produce a level of AI output quality most people don't believe is possible without expensive tools or technical knowledge.
cards.statLabel: professional techniques — you now use all of them

cards.headline: Your Module 2 technique stack
cards.body: Here's the complete toolkit you've built — with the one-line summary of when to reach for each:
bullets: 🎭 Role Prompting: When you need specialised expertise or a specific perspective
🔗 Chain of Thought: When accuracy matters or the task involves multi-step reasoning
📋 Few-Shot: When you need AI to match a specific style, format, or pattern
🔄 Iteration Loop: When the first draft is good but not great — and you want excellent
🚫 Negative Prompting: When AI's default habits are undermining your output
🏗️ Context Stacking: When you need AI to fully understand your world before it writes

cards.headline: How to combine techniques — the Power Stack
cards.body: The techniques aren't separate tools — they work together. Here's a Power Stack that uses all six in one prompt session:
bullets: 1️⃣ Start with your Context Stack (Layer 1-5 brief) — sets the full brief
2️⃣ Add a Role: "Act as a [specific expert] with experience in [domain]..."
3️⃣ Add Few-Shot examples if matching your style: "Here are 2 examples of what I want..."
4️⃣ Write your 4-ingredient prompt with Chain of Thought: "...think through this step by step."
5️⃣ Add your Do NOT list: "Do NOT: [your exclusions]"
6️⃣ Run the Iteration Loop until it's right: 2-3 targeted follow-ups
A full Power Stack takes 2 minutes to set up and produces output that would otherwise take an hour to edit.

cards.headline: What's coming in Module 3
cards.body: Module 3 is where everything becomes real. Instead of techniques in isolation, you'll apply your full toolkit to the most valuable real-world tasks:
bullets: ✍️ Lesson 15: Prompting for writing — articles, emails, copy, content at scale
🔍 Lesson 16: Prompting for research — deep dives, synthesis, competitive analysis
🎨 Lesson 17: Prompting for creativity — ideas, concepts, brainstorming, naming
💼 Lesson 18: Prompting for business — strategy, decisions, analysis, planning
📚 Lesson 19: Build your Prompt Library — your permanent competitive advantage
🚀 Lesson 20: Advanced techniques — the cutting-edge moves that 1% of users know
🎓 Lesson 21: Graduation — your final challenge and certification

cards.headline: The Module 2 Power Stack Challenge
cards.body: Your challenge: use at least 4 of the 6 techniques in a single prompt session to complete a real task you've been putting off.
bullets: Pick a task: a difficult email, a piece of content, a business analysis, a creative brief
Build your Power Stack: Context Stack + Role + Few-Shot (if needed) + 4-ingredient prompt
Add your Do NOT list. Include "think through this step by step" for any analysis.
Run 2-3 Iteration Loop passes on the first draft
Look at the final output. That's what 6 techniques combined produces.
You've just crossed the threshold from AI user to AI power user.

quiz.question: When is Role Prompting most valuable?
options: When you want AI to write in your personal style
When you need specialised expertise or a specific professional perspective in the output
When you want to make prompts shorter
When the task involves multi-step calculations
quiz.explanation: Role prompting activates domain-specific patterns from AI's training data by assigning it a specialist identity. It's most valuable when you need output that reflects a specific type of expertise — a lawyer reviewing a contract, a CFO analysing a budget, a copywriter writing an ad. It's less necessary for tasks where generic competence is sufficient and more necessary when the nuance of a specific professional perspective matters.

quiz.question: In the Power Stack, what is the correct order to build a prompt session?
options: Task first → Role → Context Stack → Few-Shot → Do NOT list
Do NOT list → Context Stack → Task → Role → Iteration
Context Stack → Role → Few-Shot examples → 4-ingredient prompt with CoT → Do NOT list → Iteration Loop
Few-Shot → Chain of Thought → Context Stack → Negative Prompting
quiz.explanation: The Power Stack builds from broadest to most specific: Context Stack sets the standing brief → Role activates the expert perspective → Few-Shot examples establish style → the 4-ingredient prompt with Chain of Thought handles the actual task → Do NOT list filters output → Iteration Loop refines. This order mirrors how a professional would brief a human expert: background first, then credentials, then examples, then the task, then quality control.

quiz.question: True or False: You should use all 6 techniques for every prompt — more techniques always means better output.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Using all 6 techniques for a simple task like "list 5 synonyms for 'happy'" is overkill — it adds complexity without improving the output. The Power Stack is for important, complex, or high-quality tasks. For quick queries, a simple well-structured prompt is faster and just as good. Match the sophistication of your approach to the importance of the task. Save the Power Stack for work that actually matters.

quiz.question: Which technique is specifically designed to prevent AI's predictable default habits from appearing in your output?
options: Role Prompting
Chain of Thought
Context Stacking
Negative Prompting
quiz.explanation: Negative prompting is purpose-built to eliminate AI's default habits — the "Certainly!", the excessive bullet points, the hedge phrases, the corporate jargon. While other techniques shape what AI produces, negative prompting directly blocks specific outputs you want to avoid. It works like a content filter you control, removing the predictable patterns that make AI output feel generic before they reach your screen.
