lessons.title: Prompting for Writing: Content at Scale
lessons.subtitle: Emails, articles, social posts, copy — the exact prompts for every writing task

cards.headline: Writing is the #1 use case for AI — and yet most people are using it at 10% of its potential. Today you get the exact prompts for every writing task you'll ever need.
cards.body: Module 3 is where your technique toolkit meets the real world. Lesson 15 is the most practically useful lesson in this course: a complete writing prompt playbook covering every major content type — with exact templates you can copy, customise, and use today.
cards.statLabel: of professionals say AI writing assistance saves them 3+ hours per week

cards.headline: Email prompts that actually work
cards.body: Email is where most people start with AI — and where most people get mediocre results. These templates produce emails you'll barely need to edit:
bullets: 📧 Follow-up: "Write a warm 3-sentence follow-up email to [name/role] who hasn't replied in [X] days. Context: [what you discussed]. Tone: friendly but gently persistent. Do NOT sound passive-aggressive."

📧 Cold outreach: "Act as a direct response copywriter. Write a 5-sentence cold email to [target] about [offer]. Lead with their pain point, not our product. CTA: [specific ask]. Tone: human and direct."
📧 Difficult message: "Write a professional email declining [request/offer] from [person/company]. Preserve the relationship. Be clear and final. Tone: warm but firm. Under 100 words."

cards.headline: Social media prompts that drive engagement
cards.body: Social content lives and dies on the hook. These prompts prioritise it:
bullets: 📱 LinkedIn post: "Write a LinkedIn post about [topic/insight]. Hook: start with a surprising fact or bold opinion — not a question. Format: 3 short paragraphs + 3 bullet points. Tone: authoritative but human. 150 words max."
📱 Twitter/X thread: "Write a 5-tweet thread about [topic]. Tweet 1: hook that stops the scroll. Tweets 2-4: one insight each. Tweet 5: strong takeaway + CTA. Each tweet under 240 chars."
📱 Instagram caption: "Write a 3-sentence Instagram caption for [image description]. Open with an emotional hook. End with a question to drive comments. Tone: [warm/inspiring/witty]."

cards.headline: Long-form content prompts — articles & blogs
cards.body: Long-form content benefits most from structure prompting. Get the structure right first, then fill each section:
bullets: 📝 Structure first: "Create an outline for a 1,000-word article on [topic] for [audience]. Format: headline, subheads, 2-sentence summary of each section. No filler — every section must deliver new value."
📝 Section by section: "Write the [intro/section 2/conclusion] of this article. [Paste outline]. For this section: [specific instruction]. Tone: [voice]. Under [X] words."
📝 SEO angle: "Rewrite this article section to naturally include the phrase '[keyword]' 2-3 times without it feeling forced. Keep tone intact."
Pro tip: Never ask AI to write a full article in one shot — section-by-section produces far better quality

cards.headline: Write something you've been putting off
cards.body: Pick one piece of writing you've been avoiding this week — an email, a post, an article section. Then:
bullets: Paste your Context Stack (from Lesson 13) to set the brief
Add the Role that fits: editor, copywriter, content strategist
Use the relevant template from today's lesson, customised for your task
Add your Do NOT list to cut AI's generic habits
Run 2 Iteration Loop passes: first for structure, then for tone
That's your real-world writing workflow. It works for everything.

quiz.question: Why is it better to write a long-form article section-by-section rather than asking AI to write the whole thing at once?
options: AI has a word limit that prevents full articles being generated
Section-by-section allows you to add specific instructions for each part, producing consistently higher quality throughout
Full articles cost more tokens
AI's attention span decreases for longer outputs, making later sections worse
quiz.explanation: When you ask AI to write a full article in one shot, it has to balance attention across the whole piece — and later sections often become thinner, more generic, or lose the thread of earlier ones. Section-by-section lets you write a structure prompt first, then give each section its own specific instructions, tone nudges, and quality check. The result is consistently high quality throughout, not just a strong opening.

quiz.question: For a cold outreach email, which of these opening approaches will produce the best result?
options: Open with who you are and your company background
Open with the recipient's pain point — what they struggle with — before mentioning your product
Open with a compliment about the recipient's company
Open with your offer and pricing immediately
quiz.explanation: The most effective cold emails lead with the reader's world — their pain, their challenge, their goal — not the sender's product. This is why the cold email prompt template instructs AI to "lead with their pain point, not our product." Opening with who you are or what you sell creates immediate friction. Opening with a problem the reader recognises creates immediate relevance. That's the difference between emails that get replies and emails that get deleted.

quiz.question: True or False: For social media posts, starting with a question is the most effective hook strategy.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False — at least for LinkedIn and most professional platforms. The LinkedIn post template specifically instructs: "Hook: start with a surprising fact or bold opinion — not a question." Questions have become so overused as hooks ("Have you ever wondered...?") that readers are now desensitised to them. Bold opinions and surprising facts stop the scroll because they create genuine tension or curiosity. On other platforms the rules differ — test what works for your specific audience.

quiz.question: What is the most important upgrade you can make to an email prompt to prevent generic, unusable output?
options: Making the prompt shorter so AI has less to misinterpret
Adding your Context Stack + specific recipient context + a Do NOT list targeting AI's email habits
Asking AI to write the email in first person
Using a role prompt: "Act as an email marketing specialist"
quiz.explanation: Generic email output almost always traces back to missing context. AI doesn't know the relationship, the history, the recipient's role, or what outcome you're aiming for — so it writes for an imaginary generic situation. Adding your Context Stack (who you are, your audience, your goal) plus specific recipient context fills those gaps. The Do NOT list then eliminates AI's email defaults — the hollow openers, the passive sign-offs, the filler sentences. Together they eliminate generic output at the source.

lessons.title: Prompting for Research: Deep Dives & Synthesis
lessons.subtitle: Turn AI into your personal research analyst — fast, thorough, and source-aware

cards.headline: What used to take a researcher three days — competitive analysis, market deep dives, synthesising dozens of sources — AI can structure in 20 minutes. If you ask it right.
cards.body: Research is one of the highest-leverage AI use cases, but it's also one of the most dangerous if you don't know how to prompt correctly. AI can hallucinate facts confidently. Today you'll learn how to get extraordinary research output — and how to verify what matters.
cards.statLabel: to complete research that once took a full day — with the right prompts

cards.headline: The research prompt formula
cards.body: Great research prompts combine role, scope, format, and a verification instruction. Here's the formula:
bullets: 🎭 Role: "Act as a [research analyst / market researcher / industry expert] specialising in [domain]"
🎯 Scope: "Research [specific topic] with a focus on [angle — trends / competitors / risks / opportunities]"
📋 Format: "Present your findings as: [executive summary + key points + sources to verify]"
✅ Verification: "For any specific statistics or claims, flag them for verification — mark with [VERIFY]"
The [VERIFY] tag is critical — it makes AI honest about what needs checking rather than presenting everything with equal confidence

cards.headline: Research prompt templates by type
cards.body: Different research tasks need different structures. Here are the four most valuable:
bullets: 🏢 Competitive analysis: "Act as a strategy consultant. Analyse [competitor] vs [our company] across: pricing, positioning, target audience, key differentiators, and weaknesses. Format: comparison table + 3 strategic insights. Flag anything needing verification with [VERIFY]."

📈 Market research: "Summarise the current state of [market/industry]: size, growth rate, key players, major trends, and biggest unmet needs. Audience: [investor/executive/founder]. Format: 5 bullet points per section. [VERIFY] all stats."

🔍 Topic deep-dive: "Give me a comprehensive overview of [topic] that would bring an intelligent non-expert up to speed. Cover: what it is, why it matters, key concepts, major debates, and practical implications. Format: structured sections with clear headers."

📊 Pros & cons analysis: "Act as a devil's advocate and balanced analyst. Give me the strongest case FOR and the strongest case AGAINST [decision/option]. No hedging — commit to the best arguments on each side."

cards.headline: The hallucination problem — and how to manage it
cards.body: AI research has one critical weakness: it sometimes states incorrect facts confidently. Here's how to use AI for research without getting burned:
bullets: ⚠️ High hallucination risk: specific statistics, publication dates, quotes, study citations, recent events (post-2024)
✅ Low hallucination risk: frameworks, general concepts, synthesis of well-established ideas, strategic analysis
🔧 Fix 1: Always add "[VERIFY] any specific statistics or claims" to research prompts
🔧 Fix 2: Use AI to structure and synthesise — use primary sources (Google, databases) for specific facts
🔧 Fix 3: Ask AI directly: "Which parts of this response are you least confident about?" — it's surprisingly honest when asked

cards.headline: Run a research deep-dive on something you need to know
cards.body: Pick a topic you've been meaning to research — a competitor, a market, a concept, a decision. Then:
bullets: Use the research formula: Role + Scope + Format + [VERIFY] instruction
Run the competitive analysis or topic deep-dive template, customised for your topic
When the output arrives, identify anything marked [VERIFY] — check those points with a quick Google
Use the output as your research skeleton — it saves hours of initial synthesis work
Notice: AI gives you the structure and connections. You supply the factual verification.

quiz.question: What does adding "[VERIFY] any specific statistics or claims" to a research prompt achieve?
options: It makes AI search the internet in real time for verified data
It instructs AI to flag claims that need checking rather than presenting everything with equal confidence
It prevents AI from including any unverified information in the response
It connects AI to academic databases for peer-reviewed sources
quiz.explanation: The [VERIFY] instruction is a pragmatic hallucination management tool. It doesn't give AI access to the internet or databases — it instructs AI to flag claims it's less certain about, separating well-established knowledge from specific facts that could be wrong. This lets you use AI for high-speed synthesis and structure while targeting your manual verification effort at the specific claims that carry risk. It's honest AI-human collaboration.

quiz.question: Which type of AI research output has the LOWEST risk of hallucination?
options: Specific statistics with exact numbers
Quotes attributed to named individuals
Frameworks, general concepts, and synthesis of well-established ideas
Publication dates and study citations
quiz.explanation: AI is most reliable when synthesising general, well-established knowledge — frameworks, broad concepts, strategic analysis, and widely understood ideas. These are densely represented in training data and don't require precise factual recall. Specific statistics, quotes, dates, and citations are high-risk because AI can generate plausible-sounding specifics that are subtly wrong. Use AI for synthesis and structure; verify specific facts independently.

quiz.question: True or False: You should ask AI to write your entire research report in one prompt, including all data, citations, and analysis.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. The best research workflow uses AI for structure and synthesis — then you verify and supplement with primary sources. A single one-shot research prompt produces a confident-sounding document that may contain subtle errors throughout. The better approach: use AI to build the skeleton (structure, key questions, analysis framework), verify specific facts independently, and use follow-up prompts to deepen each section. AI accelerates research; it doesn't replace critical thinking.

quiz.question: How can you make AI more honest about which parts of a research response it's least confident about?
options: Ask it to only include information it is 100% certain about
Use a different AI tool that has more reliable data
Ask directly: "Which parts of this response are you least confident about?"
AI cannot assess its own confidence — you must always verify everything
quiz.explanation: Modern AI models have a reasonable ability to flag their own uncertainty when directly asked — they won't volunteer it unprompted, but they will often give useful calibration when you ask. "Which parts of this response are you least confident about?" or "What should I verify before relying on this?" prompts AI to surface uncertainty it would otherwise present confidently. It's not perfect, but it's a useful final check before acting on AI research output.

lessons.title: Prompting for Creativity: Ideas, Names & Concepts
lessons.subtitle: Break creative blocks and generate 50 ideas in the time it used to take to think of one

cards.headline: The blank page is the enemy of creativity. AI eliminates it — but only if you know how to push past the obvious. Today you'll learn to prompt for genuinely original ideas.
cards.body: Most people use AI for creative tasks and get back safe, predictable, forgettable outputs. That's a prompting problem, not an AI problem. The techniques in today's lesson — divergence, constraint forcing, and perspective shifting — are what separate creative professionals from everyone else.
cards.statLabel: usable ideas in 10 minutes with divergent prompting — vs 3-5 from a typical brainstorm

cards.headline: The divergence technique — quantity before quality
cards.body: The #1 mistake in creative prompting: asking for the best idea. You can't know what's best before you've seen the options. Always ask for volume first.
bullets: ❌ Weak: "Give me a name for my app" → AI gives you 1-3 safe, generic options

✅ Strong: "Generate 30 name ideas for [app description]. Range from safe and descriptive to bold and unexpected. Include: portmanteaus, metaphors, verbs-as-names, and abstract concepts." → 30 options across the full creative spectrum
Rule: the more ideas, the higher the ceiling. The best ideas never come first.
After 30, ask: "Which 5 have the most commercial potential and why?" — use AI to filter too

cards.headline: Constraint forcing — creativity through restriction
cards.body: Paradoxically, creative work improves with constraints. Constraints force AI (and you) out of the default zone:
bullets: 🔒 Word limits: "Name ideas — one word only, max 8 letters" → Forces punchy, memorable names
🎯 Audience constraint: "Ideas that would resonate with a 22-year-old in Tokyo, not a 45-year-old in London"
🚫 Exclusion constraint: "No tech jargon, no 'AI' in the name, no compound words with 'smart'"
🌍 Cultural constraint: "Ideas that work across English, Spanish, and French without translation issues"
⏱️ Time constraint: "Campaign concepts that can be executed in under a week with no budget"
Add constraints one at a time to progressively refine — not all at once at the start

cards.headline: Perspective shifting — see the idea from new angles
cards.body: The best creative ideas often come from an unexpected viewpoint. These perspective prompts reliably unlock original thinking:
bullets: 🔄 Reversal: "What would the opposite of [concept] look like — and is that actually better?"
🏆 Role shift: "How would Apple name this product?" / "How would a 5-year-old explain this concept?"
📖 Analogy: "Find 5 analogies for [concept] from completely unrelated fields — nature, sport, cooking, architecture"
⚡ Extreme version: "What's the most outrageous, unexpected version of this idea — one that would get us press coverage just by existing?"
🎭 Enemy perspective: "If a competitor wanted to make this idea fail, what would they say about it?"

cards.headline: Run a 10-minute creative sprint
cards.body: Pick any creative challenge you're currently facing — naming something, finding a campaign hook, generating content ideas, coming up with a new product concept. Then:
bullets: Round 1 — Diverge: Ask for 25 ideas with explicit range from "safe and obvious" to "unexpected and bold"
Round 2 — Constrain: Apply 2-3 constraints to the most promising batch. Generate 15 more.
Round 3 — Shift: Use a perspective prompt on your top 3 ideas. What does the Apple version look like? The reversal?
Round 4 — Filter: Ask AI: "From everything we've generated, which 3 ideas have the highest potential and why?"
In 10 minutes you'll have a shortlist most creative teams would be happy with after a day's work.

quiz.question: Why should you ask for 25-30 ideas before filtering, rather than asking for "the best 3"?
options: AI performs better with larger output targets
The best ideas rarely come first — volume expands the creative ceiling and reveals options that weren't obvious
It uses more tokens, which produces higher quality
AI filters ideas better with a larger pool to choose from
quiz.explanation: Creative quality follows a power law: the best ideas hide in the long tail. When you ask for "the best 3", AI produces the most statistically likely — which means the most common, expected, and forgettable. When you ask for 30 and specify a range from "safe" to "unexpected", AI is forced to explore the full creative spectrum. The surprising, original options that make creative work distinctive are almost never in the first three.

quiz.question: What does "constraint forcing" do in creative prompting?
options: It limits AI's creative output to protect brand guidelines
It restricts AI to verified, fact-based creative ideas only
It applies specific limitations that paradoxically push AI outside its default creative zone into more original territory
It forces AI to always choose the safest, most commercially viable option
quiz.explanation: Constraints are creativity accelerators, not limiters. "One word, max 8 letters" forces AI out of the predictable compound-word names it defaults to. "No AI or Smart in the name" blocks the clichés. Cultural constraints push toward universally resonant ideas. Each constraint is a fence that forces AI to think in a different direction — and the ideas that emerge from those forced turns are often more original than anything that would have appeared without them.

quiz.question: You want AI to generate a brand name for a new product. Which prompt will produce the most useful creative output?
options: "Give me a brand name for my new product"
"What would be a good name?"
"Generate 30 brand name ideas for [product description]. Range from descriptive to abstract. Include: portmanteaus, verbs-as-nouns, metaphors. No jargon or compound words with 'smart'."
"Name my product something creative and memorable"
quiz.explanation: The strongest creative prompt specifies volume (30), range (descriptive to abstract), structure types to explore (portmanteaus, verbs-as-nouns, metaphors), and exclusions (no jargon, no 'smart' compounds). This forces AI to explore the full creative spectrum rather than defaulting to the safest, most common options. The vague prompts — "give me a name", "something creative" — produce generic results because they give AI no constraint or direction.

quiz.question: True or False: The reversal technique ("What would the opposite of this concept look like?") is only useful for coming up with deliberately bad ideas.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. The reversal technique is one of the most powerful perspective-shift prompts precisely because the opposite of a conventional idea is sometimes the better idea. Many breakthrough products were built on reversals: instead of going to the gym (the conventional fitness solution), a home fitness company reversed it. Instead of hiring experts (conventional consulting), platforms democratised access. Reversal prompting forces a re-examination of assumptions — and occasionally the opposite turns out to be genuinely superior.

lessons.title: Prompting for Business: Strategy & Decisions
lessons.subtitle: Use AI as a thinking partner for your toughest business challenges

cards.headline: The most valuable AI use case isn't writing emails faster — it's having a McKinsey-level strategic thinking partner available at any hour, for any problem, at no cost.
cards.body: Business prompting is different from writing prompting. The goal isn't polished prose — it's clear thinking. The best business prompts use AI as a pressure-tester, a devil's advocate, a second brain. Today you'll get the exact prompts for your most important business decisions.
cards.statLabel: the cost of a McKinsey consultant — AI gives you the same frameworks for free

cards.headline: Strategic analysis prompts
cards.body: These prompts structure complex business problems into clear, actionable frameworks:
bullets: 🔷 SWOT: "Act as a strategy consultant. Run a rigorous SWOT analysis for [business/project]. For each quadrant, give 3-5 specific points — not generic observations. Format: table. Flag anything needing market data with [VERIFY]."

🔷 Decision framework: "I need to decide between [Option A] and [Option B]. Think through this step by step. Consider: financial impact, strategic fit, execution risk, reversibility, and timing. Recommend one with a clear rationale."

🔷 Risk analysis: "Act as a senior risk officer. Identify the top 5 risks in [plan/idea]. For each: likelihood (high/med/low), impact (high/med/low), and a mitigation strategy. Be specific — not generic risk categories."

cards.headline: Stress-testing your ideas
cards.body: The most valuable business use of AI is stress-testing — finding the flaws before reality does:
bullets: 💥 Pre-mortem: "Imagine it's 18 months from now and [project/decision] has completely failed. Think through step by step what went wrong. Be specific — not abstract failure categories."
🔍 Assumption audit: "List every assumption embedded in this plan: [paste plan]. For each assumption, rate how confident you are it's correct, and what happens to the plan if it's wrong."
👹 Strongest objection: "Act as the most sceptical investor who has seen this pitch fail before. What's the single most damaging objection to [idea]? Don't hedge — give your harshest honest critique."
🎯 Second opinion: "I'm about to [decision]. What am I not thinking about? What would a contrarian say?"

cards.headline: Business planning prompts that actually help
cards.body: These turn AI into a genuine planning partner — not just a document filler:
bullets: 📋 Goal decomposition: "My goal is [big goal] by [date]. Break this down into: quarterly milestones, monthly targets, weekly actions, and the single most important thing I should do this week. Be specific and realistic."

💰 Pricing strategy: "Act as a pricing consultant. I'm launching [product/service] at [price]. Analyse: is this the right price point for [audience]? What alternatives should I consider? Use the value-based pricing framework."

📣 Go-to-market: "Act as a CMO. Build a lean go-to-market strategy for [product] targeting [audience]. Budget: [constraint]. Format: 4 phases with specific channels, messages, and success metrics for each."

🏆 Competitive positioning: "In a market with [list competitors], where is the white space for [my business]? Think through: underserved audiences, unmet needs, and positioning angles competitors have ignored."

cards.headline: Put AI on your hardest current business problem
cards.body: Think of the business decision or challenge you're most uncertain about right now. Then run it through two prompts back to back:
bullets: First: The decision framework prompt — "Think through this step by step. Consider: [key factors]. Recommend one option with a clear rationale."
Then: The pre-mortem — "Imagine this decision has completely failed in 12 months. What specifically went wrong?"
The combination of forward-looking analysis + backward-looking failure modes gives you 360° coverage
Act on the recommendation only after you've addressed the top 2 failure modes from the pre-mortem
This is how executives use AI as a thinking partner — not just a writing assistant

quiz.question: What makes the pre-mortem prompt uniquely valuable for business decisions?
options: It predicts the future with high statistical accuracy
By imagining failure has already happened, it bypasses optimism bias and surfaces specific, actionable failure modes before they occur
It uses Chain of Thought, which improves accuracy for predictions
It gives you legal protection if the project does fail
quiz.explanation: The pre-mortem is powerful because it bypasses optimism bias — the natural human tendency to underweight failure scenarios when we're excited about a plan. By setting the premise as "this has already failed", AI (and your own thinking) is freed from the need to be positive or reassuring. The result is a specific, plausible list of failure modes you can address proactively. It's one of the most practical risk-management tools available, and AI makes it available in minutes.

quiz.question: Which business prompt would best help you identify a gap in a crowded market?
options: The SWOT analysis prompt
The goal decomposition prompt
The competitive positioning prompt — "where is the white space for my business among these competitors?"
The risk analysis prompt
quiz.explanation: The competitive positioning prompt is specifically designed to find white space — underserved audiences, unmet needs, and positioning angles that existing competitors have ignored. It directs AI to look at the gaps rather than the occupied territory. SWOT is useful for analysing your own position. Risk analysis looks at downside. Goal decomposition plans execution. Competitive positioning is the right tool for identifying strategic opportunity in a crowded market.

quiz.question: True or False: AI's business strategy output can be trusted as a final answer without additional critical review.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. AI is a thinking partner and framework generator — not an oracle. Business strategy output from AI should be treated as a strong first draft: a structured analysis that surfaces options, risks, and frameworks you might not have considered. It needs your domain knowledge, current market context, and judgment to become a reliable final answer. The value of AI in business thinking is speed and structure — not replacing the decision-maker's expertise.

quiz.question: You're about to make a significant business decision and want to find flaws in your thinking. Which two prompts should you run back-to-back?
options: The SWOT analysis + the goal decomposition prompt
The go-to-market strategy + the pricing strategy prompt
The decision framework (step-by-step analysis) + the pre-mortem (imagine it's failed — what went wrong?)
The competitive positioning + the assumption audit
quiz.explanation: The decision framework + pre-mortem combination gives you 360° coverage: forward-looking structured analysis of what should happen, followed by backward-looking failure mapping of what could go wrong. Together they produce both the recommended path and the specific vulnerabilities in that path. Acting on the recommendation only after addressing the pre-mortem's top failure modes is the discipline that separates good decisions from lucky ones.

lessons.title: Build Your Prompt Library
lessons.subtitle: Your permanent competitive advantage — a personal collection that keeps getting better

cards.headline: Every prompt you've written in this course is an asset. Every prompt you write from now on can be one too. Your Prompt Library is the compound interest of AI skill.
cards.body: Most people treat each AI interaction as disposable — write, use, forget. Power users treat every great prompt like a recipe worth saving. Over time, a well-organised Prompt Library becomes your single biggest productivity advantage — a collection of proven, refined prompts that get results every time.
cards.statLabel: faster execution on repeated tasks once you have a well-stocked Prompt Library

cards.headline: What goes in a Prompt Library
cards.body: Not every prompt deserves saving — only the ones that passed the quality test. Here's how to decide:
bullets: ✅ Save it: Any prompt where the output was genuinely impressive and you'd use it again
✅ Save it: Templates you've customised for your specific context and voice
✅ Save it: Context Stacks for your major projects or clients
✅ Save it: Role combinations that reliably produce expert-level output in your field
❌ Skip it: One-off prompts for unique tasks you'll never repeat
❌ Skip it: First-draft prompts that needed heavy iteration — save the final refined version instead

cards.headline: How to organise your library
cards.body: A disorganised library is nearly as useless as no library. Use this simple structure:
bullets: 📁 Category folders: Writing · Research · Creativity · Business · Communication · Personal
📝 Each entry: Title | Use case | The prompt (with [PLACEHOLDERS] for variables) | Last updated
⭐ Star your top 10 — the ones you use most often. Keep them at the top.
🔄 Review quarterly: delete what's stale, refine what's close but not perfect
Tools: Notion, Apple Notes, Google Docs — pick the one you already live in. Complexity kills adoption.

cards.headline: Building your Starter 10
cards.body: Start with 10 high-value prompts rather than trying to save everything. Here's the ideal starter set based on what you've learned in this course:
bullets: 1. My Context Stack (Lesson 13) — your universal background brief
2. My Do NOT list (Lesson 12) — your personal exclusion block
3. Power Email — cold outreach template customised for your industry
4. Power Post — social media template in your brand voice with few-shot examples
5. Research brief — your standard competitive/market analysis template
6. Decision framework — for any significant business choice
7. Pre-mortem — for stress-testing any plan
8. Creative sprint — your 30-ideas divergence template
9. Role stack — your 3 go-to expert roles for your most common tasks
10. Iteration toolkit — your 5 favourite follow-up prompt patterns

cards.headline: Build your Starter 10 right now
cards.body: Open a new document — Notion, Google Docs, Apple Notes, wherever you'll actually use it. Then:
bullets: Create 10 entries using the list above as your template
For each one, go back through this course and pull the best version of that prompt
Add [PLACEHOLDERS] for anything that changes per task (e.g. [audience], [topic], [word count])
Star your top 3 — the prompts you'll use this week
Commit: every time you write a prompt that produces a great output, spend 60 seconds saving it
In 3 months this library will be worth more than any AI tool subscription.

quiz.question: Which of these should you save to your Prompt Library?
options: Every prompt you write, even one-off queries
Only prompts that are completely unique — never saving templates
Prompts where the output was genuinely impressive and you'd use them again, especially refined templates
Only prompts from this course — nothing you write yourself
quiz.explanation: The Prompt Library is a curation exercise, not an archive. Save prompts that passed a quality test — where the output was genuinely impressive, where you've customised a template for your specific context, or where a role combination reliably produces expert output. Skip one-offs and unrefined first drafts. Quality over quantity: 20 excellent saved prompts beats 200 mediocre ones you'll never reuse.

quiz.question: What is the single most important feature of a well-organised Prompt Library entry?
options: Including the AI's original output alongside the prompt
Using [PLACEHOLDERS] for variable elements so the template is immediately reusable
Dating every entry with the exact time it was created
Writing a long explanation of why the prompt works
quiz.explanation: [PLACEHOLDERS] are what turn a one-time prompt into a reusable template. A prompt like "Write a [format] about [topic] for [audience]. Tone: [voice]." can be used for hundreds of different tasks with minimal friction. Without placeholders, a saved prompt is just a historical record — interesting but not actionable. With placeholders, it's a precision tool you can reach for immediately. This is the single habit that determines whether a Prompt Library becomes genuinely useful.

quiz.question: Why should you start with 10 high-quality prompts rather than trying to save everything?
options: AI tools have a limit of 10 saved prompts
Complexity kills adoption — a focused starter set you actually use beats a sprawling archive you never open
More than 10 prompts creates confusion about which to use
You can only build a 10-prompt library on the free plan
quiz.explanation: The biggest enemy of a Prompt Library isn't having too few prompts — it's building something so large and unwieldy you stop using it. Starting with 10 high-quality, frequently-used prompts builds the habit of opening and using the library. Once the habit is established, you can expand. A library of 10 prompts you use daily is more valuable than 200 prompts you've never opened since saving them.

quiz.question: True or False: Your Prompt Library should be stored in a dedicated, specialised AI tool — not in a notes app you already use.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. The best Prompt Library is the one you actually open. Use whatever tool you already live in — Notion, Apple Notes, Google Docs, even a simple text file. Switching to a new specialised tool adds friction that kills the habit. The system matters less than the consistency. If you open Notion 20 times a day anyway, your Prompt Library belongs in Notion. Simplicity and familiarity always win over sophistication.

lessons.title: Advanced Techniques: The 1% Moves
lessons.subtitle: The cutting-edge prompting techniques that most users will never discover

cards.headline: You've mastered the fundamentals and the core techniques. Now here's what separates the top 1% of AI users — the moves that feel almost like cheating.
cards.body: These advanced techniques go beyond the standard toolkit. They're less well-known, require a bit more setup, and produce outputs that genuinely surprise people. By the end of this lesson you'll have moves that most AI users — including many professionals — have never heard of.
cards.statLabel: of AI users know and use all five of these advanced techniques

cards.headline: Technique 1: Self-critique prompting
cards.body: Instead of accepting AI's first output, ask AI to critique it before you see it. This builds the Iteration Loop into a single prompt:
bullets: How: After your main prompt, add: "Before giving me the final version, critique your draft. What are its 3 weaknesses? Then rewrite it addressing those weaknesses."
What happens: AI produces a draft, identifies its own flaws, and gives you an improved version — all in one step
When to use: High-stakes writing, complex analysis, any task where quality matters more than speed
Result: You get output that's already been through one iteration loop before you see it — significantly better than any raw first draft

cards.headline: Technique 2: Persona prompting
cards.body: More specific than role prompting — you assign AI a fictional but highly detailed persona with opinions, style, and history:
bullets: Role prompt: "Act as a marketing expert" → Generic expert voice

Persona prompt: "You are Alex, a CMO who built 3 startups to acquisition, writes brutally direct copy, hates buzzwords, and thinks most marketing is cowardly." → Distinct, opinionated, memorable voice
Best for: Brand voice creation, content with a strong point of view, advisory responses with real edge
Tip: Once you've built a great persona, save it in your Prompt Library for reuse across sessions

cards.headline: Techniques 3 & 4: Socratic prompting + Output seeding
cards.body: Two underused techniques that solve specific, common problems:
bullets: 🧠 Socratic prompting: Instead of asking for answers, ask AI to ask YOU questions. "Ask me the 5 most important questions you'd need answered before advising me on [decision]." Use AI to identify what you don't know.

🌱 Output seeding: Give AI the first sentence or paragraph of the output you want. "Continue this email in the same tone: 'Thanks for your patience — here's the update you've been waiting for...'" AI completes in your exact voice.
Socratic use case: Strategic decisions, creative briefs, any situation where you're not sure what questions to ask
Seeding use case: Ghostwriting, maintaining a consistent voice across long documents, continuing something you've already started

cards.headline: Technique 5: Prompt chaining
cards.body: Use the output of one prompt as the input for the next — building complex outputs through a deliberate chain of steps:
bullets: 🔗 Step 1: "Generate a research brief on [topic] — key questions, sub-topics, and angles to explore"
🔗 Step 2: "Using this brief as your guide: [paste Step 1 output], now write a detailed outline for a 1,500-word article"
🔗 Step 3: "Using this outline: [paste Step 2 output], write Section 2 in full. Tone: [voice]. 300 words."
Each step builds on verified output from the previous step — preventing errors from compounding
Best for: Long-form content, complex analysis, multi-stage creative projects, anything where quality at each step matters
Think of it as an assembly line — each station does one job well, and the final product is the sum of all stations

cards.headline: Pick one advanced technique to try today
cards.body: Don't try all five at once. Pick one that solves a current frustration:
bullets: Struggling with first drafts that need heavy editing? → Try Self-critique prompting
AI outputs sound generic and voice-less? → Try Persona prompting — build an Alex for your brand
Facing a decision and not sure what to consider? → Try Socratic prompting: "Ask me the 5 questions I need to answer"
Need AI to match your exact voice? → Try Output seeding: give it your first sentence
Building something complex that needs to be consistently high quality throughout? → Try Prompt chaining
Add whichever you try to your Prompt Library.

quiz.question: What does self-critique prompting achieve that a standard prompt doesn't?
options: It makes AI apologise for mistakes before making them
It builds the Iteration Loop into a single prompt — AI critiques its own draft and rewrites to address the flaws before you see it
It prevents AI from making any errors in the output
It uses fewer tokens by combining critique and creation
quiz.explanation: Self-critique prompting embeds a quality loop before the output reaches you. AI produces a draft, identifies its own 3 weaknesses, then rewrites addressing those weaknesses — all in one step. The output you receive has already been through one iteration cycle. For high-stakes writing or complex analysis, this technique saves significant editing time and consistently produces better first deliverables than standard prompting.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between role prompting and persona prompting?
options: Role prompting is for creative tasks; persona prompting is for business tasks
Persona prompting assigns a detailed fictional character with specific opinions and style, producing a more distinctive and opinionated voice than a generic role
They are the same technique with different names
Role prompting uses "Act as"; persona prompting uses "You are" — that's the only difference
quiz.explanation: Role prompting activates a general professional identity ("Act as a marketing expert") — useful but generic. Persona prompting goes further: you create a specific fictional character with history, opinions, stylistic quirks, and a distinct point of view. "You are Alex, a CMO who built 3 companies to exit, writes brutally direct copy, and hates buzzwords" produces a voice with real edge and personality. The extra specificity is what makes the output feel genuinely different rather than just competent.

quiz.question: When is Socratic prompting most useful?
options: When you want AI to generate questions for a quiz
When you want AI to teach you a topic using the Socratic method
When you're facing a complex decision and want AI to reveal what questions you should be asking — but haven't thought to ask
When you want to test how much AI knows about a topic
quiz.explanation: Socratic prompting flips the dynamic: instead of asking AI for answers, you ask AI to ask you questions. "Ask me the 5 most important questions you'd need answered before advising me on this decision" reveals the dimensions of a problem you might not have considered. It's especially powerful for strategic decisions and creative briefs — situations where you're not sure what you don't know. The questions themselves are often more valuable than any direct answer.

quiz.question: True or False: Prompt chaining is only useful for long-form writing projects.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Prompt chaining is valuable for any multi-stage task where quality at each step matters and errors in one step shouldn't contaminate the next. It works for complex analysis (research brief → outline → sections), business planning (goal setting → strategy → action plan → risk review), creative projects (concept → brief → execution → refinement), and product development (problem definition → solution space → prototype concept → go-to-market). The principle — build on verified output from the previous step — applies anywhere quality and complexity intersect.

quiz.question: What is the single most important habit to build in the 30 days after completing this course?
options: Reading more about AI research papers and staying current with new models
Using your Prompt Library daily and adding one new prompt each day — building the habit through daily practice
Completing another AI course immediately to reinforce the learning
Focusing exclusively on one technique until it's perfect before using others

The 30-day habit that transforms course completion into genuine mastery is daily use — opening your Prompt Library for real tasks every day, adding what works, removing what doesn't. In 30 days of daily use, you'll have a personalised system that reflects your actual work — and skills that feel automatic rather than effortful.

quiz.question: What does it mean to think in "prompts as systems" rather than questions?
options: Writing prompts in code rather than natural language
Treating prompts as structured, reusable inputs that produce predictable outputs — not one-off queries you throw away
Using AI only for systematic, repetitive tasks — not creative work
Organising prompts alphabetically in a database system
quiz.explanation: The systems mindset is the most important mindset shift in this course. A question is one-off: you ask, you get an answer, you move on. A system is reusable: a carefully structured prompt with placeholders, role, context, and quality controls that produces reliably excellent output whenever you deploy it. This is the difference between a tool user (ask → get → move on) and a craftsperson (design → refine → systematise → reuse). Your Prompt Library is the physical manifestation of this mindset.

quiz.question: True or False: After completing this course, the most skilled prompt engineers stop learning and rely entirely on what they've mastered.

False

The foundation you've built in this course is stable and transferable across any AI tool or model. But the specific techniques will evolve. The 30-day plan builds the habit of experimentation — one new technique per month, regular library reviews, teaching others — because mastery is maintained through continued practice, not achieved and then frozen.

quiz.question: What is the graduation challenge designed to prove?
